title: Binary Inspector
tagline: A static inspector that reads ELF, PE/COFF, and Mach-O files you compiled and reports their layout, names, links, and function starts.
summary: A static inspector for programs you compiled. Give it an ELF64 object, a COFF object, a PE32+ image, or a Mach-O 64 file. It reports the format, the architecture, and the sections and segments with permissions and entropy. It reports symbols with a small Itanium demangler, imports, exports, relocations, chained fixups, and strings with their section. It scores function starts against the unstripped build. It writes a JSON report, an HTML report with a byte map, and a diff between two builds.
youWillBuild: A static inspector that reads ELF, PE/COFF, and Mach-O files you compiled and reports their layout, names, links, and function starts.
skills: Detect a binary format and parse its header
Map sections and segments with permissions and entropy
Read symbol tables and demangle C++ names
Follow imports, exports, relocations, and chained fixups
Recover function starts and score them against ground truth
Publish a JSON report, an HTML byte map, and a build diff

prerequisites.title: Python 3.10+ for the inspector and the grader
Phase 13 lessons 32, 40, and 41: ELF tables, linking and loading, and C++ names
Hexadecimal arithmetic, little-endian byte order, and the struct module

stages.title: Detect the format and parse the header
stages.summary: Read the magic bytes and identify ELF64, a COFF object, a PE32+ image, or Mach-O 64. Parse the file header of each into one shape: format, architecture, kind, entry point, and the raw fields. Read the Mach-O load commands in sequence. Refuse 32-bit, big-endian, universal, and truncated files with a FormatError that names the reason.
stages.doc:
Stage 1 of 6. Read the [project README](https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch/blob/9712e323fde8cb2ec933310ac619e920e8e31017/projects/binary-inspector/README.md) first. This stage applies the ELF header reader of lesson [32](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch). It adds COFF, PE32+, and Mach-O with the tables of lesson [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries).

## What you build

You write three functions in the `formats` module:

- `detect_format(data)` reads the first bytes and returns `"elf64"`, `"coff"`, `"pe"`, or `"macho64"`.
- `parse_header(data)` returns one dictionary shape for all four formats.
- `load_commands(data)` returns the Mach-O load commands in file order.

Every later stage calls `parse_header` first. If the header is wrong, every section, symbol, and fixup after it is wrong too.

## Why it matters

A file extension does not identify a binary. A `.o` file from clang can be ELF or Mach-O. A `.obj` file is a COFF object and has no magic number at all. The inspector must decide from the bytes, and it must refuse a file it cannot read correctly. A tool that guesses and continues prints tables that look correct and are not.

All four formats in this project are little-endian. The supplied `unpack(fmt, data, offset)` helper reads one record with `struct.unpack_from` and raises `FormatError` when the record runs past the end of the file. Use it for every read, so a truncated file always fails with a message that names the offset.

## Work through one concrete case

The first 32 bytes of the stripped arm64 build are:

```text
cf fa ed fe 0c 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 02 00 00 00
12 00 00 00 a8 05 00 00 85 00 20 00 00 00 00 00
```

Read them as eight little-endian 32-bit fields (`<IiiIIIII`):

| Field | Bytes | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| magic | `cf fa ed fe` | `0xfeedfacf` | Mach-O 64, little-endian |
| cputype | `0c 00 00 01` | `0x0100000c` | arm64 (`CPU_TYPE_ARM` with the 64-bit flag) |
| filetype | `02 00 00 00` | 2 | `MH_EXECUTE`, so kind is `"executable"` |
| ncmds | `12 00 00 00` | 18 | 18 load commands follow |
| sizeofcmds | `a8 05 00 00` | 1448 | they occupy bytes 32 to 1480 |
| flags | `85 00 20 00` | `0x00200085` | `MH_NOUNDEFS`, `MH_DYLDLINK`, `MH_TWOLEVEL`, `MH_PIE` |

The load commands start at offset 32. Each starts with `cmd` and `cmdsize`. The first is `LC_SEGMENT_64` (`0x19`). The next starts at 32 plus its `cmdsize`. One of the 18 is `LC_MAIN` (`0x80000028`), whose `entryoff` is `0x5e8`. The `__TEXT` segment starts at virtual address `0x100000000`, so the entry point is `0x1000005e8`. That is the address of `_main` in the unstripped build.

The other formats follow the same pattern:

- ELF: `7f 45 4c 46`, then `EI_CLASS` 2 (64-bit) and `EI_DATA` 1 (little-endian). `e_type` 1 is relocatable. `e_machine` 62 (`0x3e`) is x86-64. The tally object has `e_shnum` 13 and `e_shstrndx` 1.
- COFF object: no magic. Bytes `64 86` are machine `0x8664`, then `0a 00` is 10 sections. `SizeOfOptionalHeader` is 0, which is what makes it an object.
- PE image: `MZ` at offset 0, `e_lfanew` at `0x3c` is `0x40`, and `PE\0\0` is at `0x40`. The optional header starts at `0x58` with magic `0x20b` (PE32+). `AddressOfEntryPoint` `0x1000` plus `ImageBase` `0x140000000` gives entry `0x140001000`.

```figure
pj-binary-inspector-1
```

Pick a format in the lab and change the fields. The lab computes the same decision that `detect_format` makes and shows which check fails first.

## Implement the contract

`detect_format(data: bytes) -> str`

- Fewer than 4 bytes: raise `FormatError`.
- `\x7fELF`: require `EI_CLASS` 2 and `EI_DATA` 1, else raise `FormatError` that says "ELF64" or "little-endian". Return `"elf64"`.
- `MZ`: read `e_lfanew` at `0x3c` and require `PE\0\0` there. Return `"pe"`.
- `0xfeedfacf` read as a little-endian word: return `"macho64"`. Raise for `0xfeedface` ("32-bit") and for `ca fe ba be` ("universal").
- Otherwise, if the first 20 bytes parse as a COFF file header with a machine in `COFF_MACHINES`, `SizeOfOptionalHeader` 0, and 1 to 96 sections, return `"coff"`.
- Anything else: raise `FormatError("unknown format: ...")`.

`parse_header(data: bytes) -> dict` returns:

```python
{
    "format": "elf64" | "coff" | "pe" | "macho64",
    "arch": "x86_64" | "arm64" | ...,
    "bits": 64,
    "endian": "little",
    "kind": "relocatable" | "executable" | "shared" | ...,
    "entry": int | None,
    "fields": {...},
}
```

Required `fields` keys, which later stages and the tests read:

- ELF: `e_type`, `e_machine`, `e_flags`, `e_phoff`, `e_phnum`, `e_shoff`, `e_shnum`, `e_shstrndx`. Raise when a header table runs past the end of the file. Also raise when an entry size is not 64 (sections) or 56 (program headers), or when `e_shstrndx` is not below `e_shnum`. `entry` is `None` for a relocatable file.
- COFF and PE: `machine`, `number_of_sections`, `time_date_stamp`, `pointer_to_symbol_table`, `number_of_symbols`, `size_of_optional_header`, `characteristics`, and `section_table` (the file offset of the first section entry).
- PE adds `magic`, `entry_rva`, `image_base`, `section_alignment`, `file_alignment`, `size_of_image`, `size_of_headers`, `subsystem`, `dll_characteristics`, `dll_flags` (names from `DLL_CHARACTERISTICS`), and `data_directories`, a dictionary from the names in `PE_DIRECTORIES` to `{"rva", "size"}` for nonzero entries only. Refuse magic `0x10b` (PE32). `kind` is `"shared"` when characteristics bit `0x2000` (DLL) is set.
- Mach-O: `cputype`, `filetype`, `ncmds`, `sizeofcmds`, `flags`, `flag_names`, and `load_commands` (the list of names).

`load_commands(data: bytes) -> list[dict]` returns one `{"cmd", "name", "offset", "size"}` per command. Use `LOAD_COMMANDS` for names and `LC_0x...` for unknown values. Raise when `sizeofcmds` runs past the file, or when a `cmdsize` is below 8, not a multiple of 8, or runs past `sizeofcmds`.

## Verify and inspect

From the repository root, initialize once, then grade:

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --init learning-artifacts/binary-inspector
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --stage 1 --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict
```

A fresh workspace fails with `not implemented yet: stage 1: implement parse_header`. The tests check all four formats, the 18 Mach-O load commands in `otool -l` order, the PE fields that `llvm-objdump -p` prints, five rejected variants, and the held-out program.

## Investigate the failure boundary

- Set the ELF `e_shoff` to a value near the end of the file. `parse_header` must raise before any section is read.
- Set the first `cmdsize` of the Mach-O file to 0. Without the size check, the loop reads the same command forever.
- Set `e_lfanew` past the end of the PE file. The `unpack` bounds check must name the offset.
- Feed a C source file. The last COFF check must refuse it, because the machine field does not match.

## Extensions

- Add ELF32 and PE32 by reading the 32-bit field layouts. Keep the output shape the same.
- Read one slice of a universal Mach-O: the fat header lists each architecture with an offset and a size.
- Decode `LC_BUILD_VERSION` into a platform and minimum OS version.

## References

- [System V gABI, ELF header](https://www.sco.com/developers/gabi/latest/ch4.eheader.html)
- [Microsoft PE Format](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format)
- [Apple mach-o/loader.h](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/loader.h)
- [Python struct module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/struct.html)

stages.title: Sections, segments, permissions, and entropy
stages.summary: List the sections of each format with name, address, file offset, size, and bytes in the file. Add an r/w/x permission string from the flags of the format. List ELF program headers and Mach-O segments. Compute Shannon entropy in bits per byte over the bytes each region holds in the file, so zero-fill regions report 0.
stages.doc:
Stage 2 of 6. This stage uses the section header table from lesson [32](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch) and the segment and section tables of the three formats from lesson [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries).

## What you build

You write five functions in the `layout` module:

- `shannon_entropy(data)` returns bits per byte, rounded to 4 decimal places.
- `sections(data)` lists every section with a permission string and the entropy of its bytes.
- `segments(data)` lists ELF program headers and Mach-O segments.
- `section_at_offset(section_list, offset)` and `section_at_address(section_list, address)` find the owner of a file offset or a virtual address. Stages 4, 5, and 6 use them.

## Why it matters

Sections tell you what the link editor made. Segments tell you what the loader maps and with which permissions. A section that is writable and executable, or a data section with entropy near 8, is a fact a reviewer must see before a release. Entropy measures how evenly the byte values spread. The maximum is 8 bits per byte, when all 256 values occur equally often, and zero padding is 0. In the fixtures, the code sections measure from 5.5 to 5.9 and the string sections from 4.0 to 4.7. The padding between segments measures 0.0. Compressed or encrypted data comes close to 8.

Each format stores permissions in a different place:

| Format | Where | Bits |
|---|---|---|
| ELF section | `sh_flags` | `SHF_WRITE 0x1`, `SHF_ALLOC 0x2`, `SHF_EXECINSTR 0x4` |
| ELF segment | `p_flags` | `PF_X 0x1`, `PF_W 0x2`, `PF_R 0x4` |
| COFF and PE section | `Characteristics` | `MEM_EXECUTE 0x20000000`, `MEM_READ 0x40000000`, `MEM_WRITE 0x80000000` |
| Mach-O segment | `initprot`, `maxprot` | `VM_PROT_READ 1`, `VM_PROT_WRITE 2`, `VM_PROT_EXECUTE 4` |

An ELF section without `SHF_ALLOC` is not loaded, so its string is `"---"`. A Mach-O section has no permission bits of its own. It takes `initprot` of the segment with the same name. In a Mach-O object the only segment has an empty name, so use the instruction attributes (`0x80000400`) for `"r-x"` and the table `MACHO_SEGMENT_PERMS` for the rest.

## Work through one concrete case

The ELF object for the tally program has 13 section headers of 64 bytes at `e_shoff` 1320. Entry 2 is `.text`. Its `sh_flags` is `0x6`, so `SHF_ALLOC` and `SHF_EXECINSTR` are set and `SHF_WRITE` is clear: `"r-x"`. Its `sh_offset` is 64 and `sh_size` is `0x13c` (316). Entry 5 is `.bss` with type `SHT_NOBITS` (8). Its size is 4, but it holds no bytes in the file. So `file_size` is 0 and its entropy is 0.0.

Now compute entropy for the 15-byte string `tally report v3`. Count each byte value:

| Byte | Count | p | p log2(1/p) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `t`, `l`, `r`, space | 2 each | 2/15 | 0.3876 each |
| `a`, `y`, `e`, `p`, `o`, `v`, `3` | 1 each | 1/15 | 0.2605 each |

The sum is 4 × 0.3876 + 7 × 0.2605 = 3.3736 bits per byte. The bytes `aabb` give exactly 1.0, and the 256 values 0 to 255 once each give exactly 8.0.

On the arm64 executable, `__TEXT,__text` is 768 bytes with entropy 5.8595, `__TEXT,__cstring` is 4.6413, and `__DATA,__common` is zerofill with `file_size` 0. The `__PAGEZERO` segment maps 4 GiB with no file bytes and permission `"---"`.

```figure
pj-binary-inspector-2
```

Move the sliders to set how many distinct byte values a region holds and how often the most common one appears. The lab computes the entropy and the permission string from the flag bits you select.

## Implement the contract

`shannon_entropy(data: bytes) -> float`: return 0.0 for empty input. Otherwise H = sum over byte values of p × log2(1/p), with p = count / length, rounded with `round(value, 4)`.

`sections(data: bytes) -> list[dict]`, one dictionary per section with exactly these keys:

| Key | ELF | COFF object | PE image | Mach-O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `index` | header index (skip index 0) | 1-based | 1-based | 1-based across all segments |
| `name` | from `.shstrtab` | 8-byte name, or `/n` into the string table | same | `sectname` |
| `segment` | `None` | `None` | `None` | `segname` |
| `type` | `ELF_SECTION_TYPES` name | `"code"`, `"initialized"`, `"uninitialized"`, `"other"` | same | `MACHO_SECTION_TYPES` name |
| `addr` | `sh_addr` | 0 | `ImageBase + VirtualAddress` | `addr` |
| `offset` | `sh_offset` | `PointerToRawData`, or 0 with no file bytes | same | `offset`, or 0 for zerofill |
| `size` | `sh_size` | `SizeOfRawData` | `VirtualSize` | `size` |
| `file_size` | 0 for `NOBITS`, else `sh_size` | 0 for uninitialized data | `min(SizeOfRawData, VirtualSize)` | 0 for zerofill types |
| `perms` | from `sh_flags` | from `Characteristics` | same | from the segment |
| `code` | `SHF_EXECINSTR` | `CNT_CODE 0x20` or `MEM_EXECUTE` | same | instruction attributes |
| `entropy` | of `data[offset:offset + file_size]` | same | same | same |

Raise `FormatError` when the file bytes of a section run past the end of the file. Also raise when a Mach-O `LC_SEGMENT_64` is too small for its `nsects` entries of 80 bytes.

`segments(data: bytes) -> list[dict]` returns `{"name", "addr", "size", "offset", "file_size", "perms", "max_perms", "entropy"}`. ELF names come from `ELF_SEGMENT_TYPES` and `max_perms` is `None`. Mach-O uses `segname`, `vmsize`, `initprot`, and `maxprot`. Relocatable ELF, COFF objects, and PE images return `[]`, because a PE image maps each section directly.

`section_at_offset(section_list, offset)` returns the section with the smallest `file_size` whose file range holds the offset, or `None`. `section_at_address(section_list, address)` returns the first section whose `[addr, addr + size)` holds the address, or `None`.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --stage 2 --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict
```

The tests compare names, sizes, and offsets with `llvm-objdump -h` and `otool -l` output for the same files, and check the entropy values above.

## Investigate the failure boundary

- Set the `sh_offset` of `.text` near the end of the file. `sections` must raise before it computes entropy over a short slice.
- Raise `nsects` of the Mach-O `__PAGEZERO` command to 40. The command is 72 bytes, so the section entries would overlap the next command.
- Compare `.bss` and `__common`. A tool that reads `size` bytes for a zero-fill section reports entropy for bytes that belong to another region.
- Look at `__DATA_CONST`. Its `initprot` is `"rw-"` in the file. The `SG_READ_ONLY` flag tells dyld to make it read-only after it applies the fixups of stage 4.

## Extensions

- Flag every region that is both writable and executable.
- Add a sliding-window entropy profile of 256 bytes for the code section.
- Read the ELF `GNU_RELRO` program header and report which sections it covers.

## References

- [System V gABI, sections](https://www.sco.com/developers/gabi/latest/ch4.sheader.html) and [program header](https://www.sco.com/developers/gabi/latest/ch5.pheader.html)
- [Microsoft PE Format, section flags](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format#section-flags)
- [Apple mach-o/loader.h](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/loader.h)
- [Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication", 1948](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf)

stages.title: Symbols, string tables, and demangled names
stages.summary: Read ELF .symtab and .dynsym, COFF symbol records with their auxiliary entries, and Mach-O nlist_64 entries. Resolve each name through its string table with a bounds-checked C string read. Report value, size, kind, binding, and section. Demangle a documented subset of Itanium C++ names and return None for anything outside it.
stages.doc:
Stage 3 of 6. This stage reads the ELF symbol records of lesson [32](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch) and the COFF and Mach-O symbol tables of lesson [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries). The C++ names come from lesson [41](/learn/41-recovering-data-and-types).

## What you build

You write three functions in the `symbols` module:

- `read_cstring(data, offset, end=None)` reads one NUL-terminated name and refuses a name that has no terminator before `end`.
- `demangle(name)` turns a supported Itanium C++ name into its source form, or returns `None`.
- `symbols(data)` returns every symbol of the file in one shape.

## Why it matters

Symbols are the names a reviewer reads first: which functions a build defines, which ones it needs from elsewhere, and what strip removed. All three formats store names as offsets into a string table. A name offset that points outside its table is the most common corruption in a damaged file. A reader that does not check it prints text from some other table.

The three record layouts:

| Format | Record | Size | Fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| ELF `Elf64_Sym` | `<IBBHQQ` | 24 | name offset, info (binding high 4 bits, type low 4 bits), other, section index, value, size |
| COFF symbol | `<8sIhHBB` | 18 | short name or `0` plus string table offset, value, section number (signed), type, storage class, auxiliary count |
| Mach-O `nlist_64` | `<IBBHQ` | 16 | string offset, `n_type`, `n_sect`, `n_desc`, value |

## Work through one concrete case

ELF. The `.symtab` of the tally object starts at offset 488. Entry 9 is:

```text
59 00 00 00 12 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 92 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
```

Name offset `0x59` into `.strtab` (offset 1064) gives `tally_sum`. Info `0x12` is binding 1 (`"global"`) and type 2 (`"func"`). Section index 2 is `.text`. Value 0, size `0x92` (146). `llvm-objdump -t` prints `0000000000000000 g F .text 0000000000000092 tally_sum`.

COFF. Record 28 of the COFF object is `00 00 00 00 6c 00 00 00 a0 00 00 00 01 00 20 00 02 00`. The first four bytes are zero, so the name is at offset `0x6c` in the string table that follows the 36 records: `tally_scale`. Value `0xa0`, section 1 (`.text`), type `0x20` (function), storage class 2 (external, so `"global"`), no auxiliary records. A section symbol such as `.text` has one auxiliary record. Skip it, and keep the raw index of each record, because relocations in stage 4 count auxiliary records too.

Mach-O. Entry 9 of the executable is `62 00 00 00 0f 01 00 00 40 07 00 00 01 00 00 00`. `n_type` `0x0f` is `N_SECT 0x0e` plus `N_EXT 0x01`: defined, global. `n_sect` 1 is `__text`, which holds instructions, so the kind is `"func"`. Value `0x100000740`. Entry 14 is `_puts` with `n_type` 1 (undefined, external) and `n_desc` `0x0100`. Bits 8 to 15 of `n_desc` hold library ordinal 1, the first `LC_LOAD_DYLIB`.

C++. `names.cpp` compiles to `_ZN5tally5resetEPNS_7CounterE`. Parse it:

1. `_Z` starts an encoding. `N ... E` is a nested name: `5tally`, `5reset`. Record `tally` as substitution `S_`. The last part of a function name is not recorded.
2. Parameters follow. `P` is a pointer to the next type.
3. `N S_ 7Counter E` is a nested name. `S_` expands to `tally`, then `Counter`. Record `tally::Counter` as `S0_`.
4. The pointer type `tally::Counter*` becomes `S1_`.

Result: `tally::reset(tally::Counter*)`, the same text that `c++filt` prints.

```figure
pj-binary-inspector-3
```

Type a mangled name in the lab. It shows each token, the substitution table as it grows, and the result.

## Implement the contract

`read_cstring(data: bytes, offset: int, end: int | None = None) -> str`: raise `FormatError` when `offset` is outside `[0, end)` or there is no NUL before `end`. Decode UTF-8 with replacement.

`demangle(name) -> str | None`. Supported subset:

- `_Z` and the Mach-O form `__Z`.
- Plain and nested names (`N ... E`), const member functions (`NK`), constructors `C1` `C2` `C3` and destructors `D1` `D2` `D3`, and `St` for `std::`.
- Builtin types `v b c a h s t i j l m x y f d e w z`, and `P`, `R`, `O`, `K` (pointer, reference, rvalue reference, const). Print `K` as a suffix: `char const*`.
- Substitutions `S_`, `S0_`, `S1_`, and so on, with base 36 digits.
- A function with the single parameter `v` prints `()`.
- Return `None` for a name that is not mangled, for a non-string, and for anything outside the subset, such as templates (`I ... E`) or an undefined substitution. Never raise.

`symbols(data: bytes) -> list[dict]`, one dictionary per symbol:

```python
{"index": int, "name": str, "demangled": str | None, "value": int, "size": int | None,
 "kind": "func" | "object" | "section" | "file" | "notype" | ..., "binding": "local" | "global" | "weak",
 "section": str | None, "defined": bool, "table": "symtab" | "dynsym" | "coff" | "nlist"}
```

- ELF: read every `SYMTAB` and `DYNSYM` section, skip entry 0, and take the string table from `sh_link`. Section index 0 is undefined (`None`), `0xfff1` is `"*ABS*"`, `0xfff2` is `"*COMMON*"`. An unnamed section symbol takes its section's name.
- COFF: section number above 0 names a section, -1 is `"*ABS*"`, -2 is `"*DEBUG*"`, and 0 with a nonzero value on an external symbol is `"*COMMON*"`. Storage class 103 is `"file"`. A static symbol with the section's own name and an auxiliary record is `"section"`. Type `0x20` is `"func"`. A PE image has no symbol table, so return `[]`.
- Mach-O: skip debug entries (`n_type & 0xe0`). `N_SECT` names a section, `N_ABS` is `"*ABS*"`, an undefined external with a nonzero value is `"*COMMON*"`. Add `library_ordinal` (bits 8 to 15 of `n_desc`) to undefined symbols.
- `defined` is `section is not None`.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --stage 3 --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict
```

The tests compare names, values, sizes, bindings, and sections with `llvm-objdump -t` and `nm -m`, and the demangled names with `c++filt`.

## Investigate the failure boundary

- Set the name offset of ELF entry 1 to `0x7ffffff0`. `symbols` must raise. It must not return an empty name.
- Compare the unstripped and stripped arm64 builds. Strip keeps five records: four undefined imports that dyld needs to bind, and `__mh_execute_header`, which is referenced dynamically. The stripped dylib keeps no records at all.
- Try `_Z1fS_`. There is no substitution yet, so the demangler must return `None`.
- MSVC names such as `??_C@_03IMLOALHE@low?$AA@` use a different scheme. The demangler returns `None` for them.

## Extensions

- Add template arguments (`I ... E`) and template parameters (`T_`).
- Read the ELF `.gnu.version` table and attach `@GLIBC_2.2.5` style versions to `.dynsym` names.
- Print the COFF auxiliary section record: length, relocation count, checksum, and COMDAT selection.

## References

- [System V gABI, symbol table](https://www.sco.com/developers/gabi/latest/ch4.symtab.html)
- [Microsoft PE Format, COFF symbol table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format#coff-symbol-table)
- [Apple mach-o/nlist.h](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/nlist.h)
- [Itanium C++ ABI, mangling](https://itanium-cxx-abi.github.io/cxx-abi/abi.html#mangling)

stages.title: Imports, exports, relocations, and chained fixups
stages.summary: Read ELF RELA records, COFF relocation records, Mach-O relocation_info, and PE base relocations. Read the PE import and export directories. Decode Mach-O chained fixups word by word into binds and rebases, and read the exports trie with ULEB128 values. Every pointer is checked before it is followed, and a chain or trie that loops or leaves its page fails.
stages.doc:
Stage 4 of 6. This stage implements the linkage tables of lesson [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries): relocation records, PE import and export directories, Mach-O chained fixups, and the exports trie. The relocation fields come from lesson [32](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch).

## What you build

You write five functions in the `linkage` module:

- `uleb128(data, offset)` decodes one unsigned LEB128 value.
- `relocations(data)` lists ELF, COFF, and Mach-O relocation records and PE base relocations.
- `imports(data)` lists what the file needs from elsewhere and the slots that receive each address.
- `exports(data)` lists what the file offers to others.
- `chained_fixups(data)` decodes every fixup word of a linked Mach-O file.

## Why it matters

The bytes of a call or a pointer in an object file are often zero. The relocation record says what the link editor writes there. In a linked image, the loader fills import slots before the program runs. On current macOS, the fixup information sits inside the pointer slots themselves, as chained 64-bit words. A disassembler that reads one of those slots without decoding it reports a pointer to an address that does not exist. Lesson 40 opens with that exact mistake.

The record layouts:

| Format | Record | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| ELF `Elf64_Rela` | `<QQq`, 24 bytes | offset, `r_info` (symbol index high 32 bits, type low 32 bits), addend |
| COFF relocation | `<IIH`, 10 bytes | offset, raw symbol index, type. No addend field. |
| Mach-O `relocation_info` | `<iI`, 8 bytes | address, then symbolnum:24, pcrel:1, length:2, extern:1, type:4 |
| PE base relocation block | `<II` then `<H` entries | page RVA, block size, then type (top 4 bits) and page offset (low 12 bits) |

## Work through one concrete case

ELF. The first `.rela.text` record of the tally object has offset `0x15`, `r_info` `0x0000000a00000002` (symbol index 10, type 2), and addend -4. Type 2 is `R_X86_64_PC32`. Symbol 10 is `tally_counter`. `llvm-objdump -r` prints `0000000000000015 R_X86_64_PC32 tally_counter-0x4`.

PE imports. The import directory of the small PE image is at RVA `0x2000`, which the `.rdata` section maps to file offset `0x400`. The 20-byte descriptor reads: lookup table `0x2028`, time stamp 0, forwarder 0, name `0x2096`, address table `0x2048`. The name RVA gives `kernel32.dll`. The lookup table holds three 64-bit entries and a zero. Bit 63 is clear in each, so each is the RVA of a hint and a name: hint 0 `GetStdHandle`, hint 1 `WriteConsoleA`, hint 2 `ExitProcess`. The slot of import *i* is `ImageBase + 0x2048 + 8 * i`: `0x140002048`, `0x140002050`, `0x140002058`.

Mach-O chained fixups. `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS` points at 152 bytes in `__LINKEDIT`. The header is seven 32-bit fields:

```text
00 00 00 00  20 00 00 00  50 00 00 00  60 00 00 00  04 00 00 00  01 00 00 00  00 00 00 00
version 0    starts 32    imports 80   symbols 96   count 4      format 1     names 0
```

At offset 32, `seg_count` is 5, with one start offset per segment. Only segment 2 (`__DATA_CONST`) has one, 24. At 32 + 24, `dyld_chained_starts_in_segment` reads: size 24, page size `0x4000`, pointer format 6 (`DYLD_CHAINED_PTR_64_OFFSET`), segment offset `0x4000`, page count 1, page start 0.

The chain starts at the file offset of `__DATA_CONST` (`0x4000`) plus page 0 plus 0. Read each 64-bit word:

| Offset | Raw | Bit 63 | next (bits 51 to 62) | Decoded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x4000` | `0x8010000000000000` | 1, bind | 2 (8 bytes) | ordinal 0 |
| `0x4018` | `0x8010000000000003` | 1, bind | 2 | ordinal 3 |
| `0x4020` | `0x001000000000098d` | 0, rebase | 2 | target `0x98d` + `0x100000000` |
| `0x4038` | `0x000000000000099a` | 0, rebase | 0, end | target `0x10000099a` |

The imports table at offset 80 holds 32-bit entries: library ordinal (8 bits), weak (1 bit), name offset (23 bits). Entry 3 is `0x5c01`: ordinal 1, not weak, name offset 46, and offset 96 + 46 holds `_puts`. Library ordinal 1 is the first `LC_LOAD_DYLIB`, `/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib`. So the slot at `0x100004018` receives the address of `_puts`, exactly as `dyld_info -fixups` prints.

The exports trie of the dylib starts `00 01 5f 74 61 6c 6c 79 5f 00 53`: terminal size 0, one child, edge `_tally_`, child at offset `0x53`. Each terminal node holds ULEB128 flags and a ULEB128 offset from the image base. `_tally_sum` is at `0x4a8`. Strip removes `LC_SYMTAB` records from the dylib but keeps this trie, because dyld binds through it.

```figure
pj-binary-inspector-4
```

Enter a 64-bit fixup word in the lab. It splits the word into its bit fields, decides bind or rebase, and computes the next offset and the target.

## Implement the contract

`uleb128(data: bytes, offset: int) -> tuple[int, int]`: return the value and the offset after it. Raise `FormatError` when the bytes end before a byte without bit 7, or after 10 bytes.

`relocations(data: bytes) -> list[dict]`, each `{"section", "offset", "type", "symbol", "addend"}`:

- ELF: every `RELA` (24 bytes, explicit addend) and `REL` (16 bytes, addend `None`) section. `section` is the name of `sh_info`, the section being patched. Symbols come from the table in `sh_link`. Type names are `R_X86_64_` or `R_AARCH64_` plus the name in the supplied table, or the number.
- COFF: records of each section in table order, type `IMAGE_REL_AMD64_` plus the name, addend `None`. The symbol index counts auxiliary records.
- PE: base relocations from the `basereloc` directory. Skip type 0 (padding). `offset` is the RVA, `symbol` is `None`, type `IMAGE_REL_BASED_DIR64` for type 10.
- Mach-O: records of each section. An `ARM64_RELOC_ADDEND` record (type 10) carries a signed 24-bit addend for the next record and is not listed. When `extern` is 0, `symbolnum` is a 1-based section number.
- Raise `FormatError` when a record names a symbol or a section that does not exist.

`imports(data: bytes) -> list[dict]`, each `{"name", "library", "slots", "hint", "ordinal"}`:

- PE: one row per lookup table entry. Bit 63 set means import by ordinal (`name` is `"#n"`). `slots` holds the absolute address of the IAT slot.
- Mach-O with chained fixups: one row per chained import, `ordinal` is its index, `slots` lists the addresses of the binds that use it.
- Everything else: undefined global symbols from stage 3, once per name, `slots` empty. Mach-O rows take `library` from `library_ordinal`.

`exports(data: bytes) -> list[dict]`, each `{"name", "address", "ordinal", "forwarder"}`:

- PE: the export directory. Name *k* maps to address entry `ordinals[k]`, and the exported ordinal is that index plus the ordinal base. An address inside the export directory is a forwarder string.
- Mach-O with a nonempty `LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE`: the trie, sorted by name, address = `__TEXT` base + offset.
- Everything else: defined global and weak symbols, excluding section, file, `*ABS*`, and `*DEBUG*` entries. Use `.dynsym` alone when the file has one.

`chained_fixups(data: bytes) -> dict` returns `{"header", "imports", "fixups"}`. For a file without `LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS`, return `{"header": None, "imports": [], "fixups": []}`.

- `header`: `{"version", "imports_count", "imports_format", "pointer_formats"}`.
- `imports`: `{"index", "name", "library", "weak", "addend"}`. Support import formats 1, 2, and 3. Library ordinals `0`, `-1`, and `-2` are `"self"`, `"main-executable"`, and `"flat-lookup"`.
- `fixups`: `{"offset", "address", "section", "raw", "next", "kind"}` plus `ordinal`, `name`, `library`, `addend` for a bind, or `target` for a rebase. Support pointer formats 2 and 6. Format 6 adds the `__TEXT` base to the target.
- Raise `FormatError` for a nonzero version, compressed names, an unsupported format, and a multi-start page. Also raise for a bind ordinal outside the imports table and for a chain that leaves its page.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --stage 4 --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict
```

The tests compare with `llvm-objdump -r`, `llvm-objdump -p`, and `dyld_info -fixups -exports`, and feed corrupted chains, tries, and relocation records.

## Investigate the failure boundary

- Set the `next` field of the first fixup word to `0xfff`. The next word would be `0x3ffc` bytes on, past the page. Without the page check, the reader follows pointers into unrelated data.
- Set a bind ordinal to 50 with only 4 imports. The decoder must raise. It must not print a name from past the table.
- Point a trie child back at offset 0. A reader without a visited set loops forever.
- Look at the COFF relocation for `bucket_names` at `0x102` and the ELF record at the same place. The ELF record carries addend -4. The COFF type `REL32` has the -4 built in.

## Extensions

- Decode `LC_DYLD_INFO_ONLY` bind opcodes for files linked with `-no_fixup_chains`.
- Read the ELF `.dynamic` section and list `DT_NEEDED` libraries for a shared object.
- Read the PE delay-load import directory.

## References

- [System V gABI, relocation](https://www.sco.com/developers/gabi/latest/ch4.reloc.html) and [AMD64 psABI](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI)
- [Microsoft PE Format: COFF relocations, the .idata and .edata sections, base relocations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format)
- [Apple dyld, mach-o/fixup-chains.h](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/dyld/blob/main/include/mach-o/fixup-chains.h)
- [Apple mach-o/loader.h, exports trie](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/loader.h)
- [DWARF 5, section 7.6, LEB128](https://dwarfstd.org/doc/DWARF5.pdf)

stages.title: Strings with sections and recovered function starts
stages.summary: Extract ASCII and UTF-16LE strings and name the section and segment that hold each one. Find function starts with five methods: symbols, LC_FUNCTION_STARTS, a prologue scan, direct call targets, and the entry point. Score each method against the symbol table of the unstripped build with precision and recall.
stages.doc:
Stage 5 of 6. This stage implements the function start methods of lesson [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries). It scores them as that lesson does, against the symbol table of the unstripped build.

## What you build

You write three functions in the `discovery` module:

- `extract_strings(data, section_list, segment_list=(), min_length=4)` finds printable ASCII and UTF-16LE runs and names the section and segment that hold each one.
- `function_starts(data)` returns the start addresses that five separate methods find.
- `score_starts(found, truth)` compares one method with the ground truth.

## Why it matters

`strings` without section names mixes format strings from `__cstring`, symbol names from `__LINKEDIT`, and random runs inside machine code. With the section beside each string, you can tell which strings the program prints and which ones the loader reads.

After strip, a disassembler must decide where functions begin. Each method sees a different part of the truth, and each method fails in a known way. Score each method against a build where you know the answer. You get two numbers: precision (how many reported starts are real) and recall (how many real starts it reported).

| Method | Source | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| symbols | defined function symbols inside code sections | strip removed them |
| function starts table | `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` ULEB128 deltas | the format has no such table |
| prologues | `sub sp, sp, #imm` or `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-n]!` on arm64; `push rbp; mov rbp, rsp` or `endbr64` on x86-64 | the compiler emits no frame, for example a leaf function at `-O2` |
| call targets | arm64 `bl` and x86-64 `e8` targets inside code sections | nothing calls the function, for example `main` |
| entry | `e_entry`, `AddressOfEntryPoint`, `LC_MAIN` | only one function is the entry |

## Work through one concrete case

`LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` of the stripped arm64 build points at these bytes in `__LINKEDIT`:

```text
e8 0b  d8 02  88 02  20  28  24  00
```

Each value is a ULEB128 delta. The first delta is from the `__TEXT` address `0x100000000`:

| Bytes | Delta | Start |
|---|---|---|
| `e8 0b` | `0x5e8` | `0x1000005e8` |
| `d8 02` | `0x158` | `0x100000740` |
| `88 02` | `0x108` | `0x100000848` |
| `20` | `0x20` | `0x100000868` |
| `28` | `0x28` | `0x100000890` |
| `24` | `0x24` | `0x1000008b4` |
| `00` | end | |

The unstripped build has six function symbols at those addresses: `_main`, `_tally_sum`, `_tally_scale`, `_tally_bucket`, `_tally_name`, `_tally_checksum`. Precision 1.0, recall 1.0. `_banner` sits in `__TEXT,__const`, which holds no instructions, so it is not a function start.

Call targets. The word at `0x100000628` is `46 00 00 94`, read as `0x94000046`. The top six bits `100101` mean `bl`. The low 26 bits are 70, times 4 is `0x118`, so the target is `0x100000740`, the start of `_tally_sum`. The `bl` instructions that target `__stubs` (`printf`, `puts`) are dropped, because the stubs are not functions of this program. Five targets remain. Nothing calls `main`, so recall is 5/6 = 0.8333.

Prologues. The first word of `main` is `ff 83 01 d1`, `0xd10183ff`, which matches `(word & 0xff0003ff) == 0xd10003ff`: `sub sp, sp, #0x60`. The five tally functions at `-O2` are leaf functions with no stack frame, so the scan finds 1 of 6: recall 0.1667. At `-O0` it finds 6 of 6. On the x86-64 ELF objects, `push rbp; mov rbp, rsp` finds 5 of 5 at `-O0` and 0 of 5 at `-O2`.

The `recovered` list is the union of the function starts table, the call targets, and the entry. It leaves out prologues, because a prologue pattern is the only method here that can match bytes inside a function.

```figure
pj-binary-inspector-5
```

In the lab, choose a build and the methods to combine, and add false positives. The lab computes true positives, precision, and recall from the same six addresses.

## Implement the contract

`extract_strings(data, section_list, segment_list=(), min_length=4) -> list[dict]`

- Raise `ValueError` when `min_length` is below 1.
- ASCII: runs of bytes `0x20` to `0x7e` and tab, at least `min_length` long. A run at the end of the file counts.
- UTF-16LE: runs of a printable byte followed by `0x00`, at least `min_length` characters.
- Each item is `{"offset", "text", "encoding", "section", "segment"}`, sorted by offset. `section` comes from `section_at_offset`. `segment` is the section's segment, or the segment whose file range holds the offset, or `None`.

`function_starts(data) -> dict` with sorted, unique integer lists under these keys:

- `symbols`: values of defined `"func"` symbols whose section is a code section and whose value lies inside it. In a relocatable file these are section offsets.
- `function_starts_table`: decoded `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS`, `[]` for other formats.
- `prologues`: pattern matches inside code sections only. Scan arm64 at 4-byte steps.
- `call_targets`: `[]` for a relocatable file, because its call displacements are still zero. Otherwise targets inside code sections.
- `entry`: `[header["entry"]]` or `[]`.
- `recovered`: union of `function_starts_table`, `call_targets`, and `entry`.

A code section has `code` true, file bytes, and a name outside `__stubs`, `__auth_stubs`, `__stub_helper`, `.plt`, and `.plt.sec`.

`score_starts(found, truth) -> dict` returns `{"found", "truth", "true_positives", "false_positives", "missed", "precision", "recall"}`. Count unique addresses. `false_positives` and `missed` are sorted lists. Precision is 0.0 when nothing was found. Recall is 1.0 when the truth is empty. Round both to 4 places.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --stage 5 --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict
```

The function start addresses in the tests match `nm -n` of the unstripped build and `dyld_info -function_starts` of the stripped build.

## Investigate the failure boundary

- Write `0xd10083ff` into the middle of `main`. The prologue scan reports a false positive at that address and its precision drops to 0.5. The score shows the cost of the method.
- Write the same word into `__TEXT,__const`. The scan must ignore it, because the section holds no instructions.
- Truncate `LC_FUNCTION_STARTS` to one byte `0x80`. The ULEB128 reader must raise.
- List the strings of the stripped executable in `__LINKEDIT`. The 160 bytes of `LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE` still hold the edges `hecksum`, `ounter`, `cale`, `bucket`, `main`, and `tally_`. Strip rewrote the root node so that only `__mh_execute_header` is reachable, and left the old nodes in place. The string scan finds them. The trie reader of stage 4 does not, because no reachable node points at them.

## Extensions

- Add a FLIRT-shaped signature, as lesson 40 shows. Mask the relocated bytes of each function in the object files, then match the result at each recovered start.
- Use the `.pdata` section of a linked PE image as one more method: each `RUNTIME_FUNCTION` entry names a function start.
- Report the gap between consecutive starts as an upper bound on each function size.

## References

- [Apple ld64 and dyld, LC_FUNCTION_STARTS in mach-o/loader.h](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/loader.h)
- [Arm A64 instruction set: BL, SUB (immediate), STP](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0602/latest/)
- [Andriesse, Slowinska, Bos, "Compiler-Agnostic Function Detection in Binaries", EuroS&P 2017](https://danielandriesse.com/papers/eurosp-2017.pdf)
- [Ghidra AARCH64 function start patterns](https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/master/Ghidra/Processors/AARCH64/data/patterns/AARCH64_LE_patterns.xml)

stages.title: JSON report, HTML byte map, and build diff
stages.summary: Compose every stage into one versioned JSON report and validate it. Render a standalone HTML report with a byte map. Each file slice takes its color from its region and its brightness from its entropy. Every string from the binary is escaped. Diff two reports to show section growth, moved and removed symbols, and changed imports, exports, and strings.
stages.doc: Stage 6 of 6. This stage composes stages 1 to 5 into three artifacts: a versioned JSON report, a standalone HTML page, and a diff between two builds. Lessons [32](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch) and [40](/learn/40-linking-loading-and-stripped-binaries) compare builds by hand in their labs. This stage makes that comparison one command. ## What you build You write six functions in the `report` module: - `byte_map(data, section_list, segment_list=(), cells=128)` divides the file into equal slices and labels each one. - `build_report(data, name="input", truth=None, min_string=4, cells=128)` returns the full report. - `validate_report(report)` returns a list of problems, empty when the report is valid. - `render_html(report)` returns one standalone HTML page. - `diff_reports(old, new)` compares two reports. - `render_diff_text(diff)` prints the diff as lines. The supplied CLI calls them: ```bash python3 cli.py inspect FILE [--truth UNSTRIPPED] [--json PATH] [--html PATH] [--min-string N] [--cells N] python3 cli.py diff OLD NEW [--json PATH] ``` It exits 0 on success and 2 with `error: ...` on standard error for an unreadable or unsupported file. ## Why it matters A report that only prints to a terminal cannot go into CI or a review thread. The JSON report has a schema name, so a later script can refuse a report it does not understand. The HTML page shows where the bytes are. In a byte map, a large zero-filled segment, a high-entropy blob, or a code section that grew is visible at once. Every string in the page comes from the binary, so the page escapes all of them. A binary is input you do not control, even when you compiled it. ## Work through one concrete case The stripped arm64 build is 50,264 bytes. With 128 cells, cell *i* covers `[i × 50264 // 128, (i + 1) × 50264 // 128)`: | Cell | Range | Region | Entropy | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | 0 to 392 | `headers` | 2.1376 | | 3 | 1178 to 1570 | `__text` | 3.4159 | | 5 | 1963 to 2356 | `__text` | 5.9288 | | 6 | 2356 to 2748 | `__cstring` | 2.4591 | | 7 | 2748 to 3141 | `__TEXT` | 0.0 | | 127 | 49871 to 50264 | `__LINKEDIT` | 5.9962 | The region rule: the section with the largest overlap wins. Cell 3 overlaps `__text` (which starts at 1512) by 58 bytes and no other section, so it is `__text`. A cell with no section overlap that ends at or before the first section is `headers`. Otherwise the segment with the largest overlap names it, and with no segment it is `unmapped`. Cell 7 is the zero padding at the end of `__TEXT`. The lengths add up to the file size, and each cell starts where the previous one ends. The HTML page draws one square per cell. The hue comes from the region name, and the opacity is `0.25 + 0.75 × entropy / 8`, so cell 7 is faint and cell 5 is bright. The diff of the `-O0` and `-O2` builds: ```text tally-arm64-O0 -> tally-arm64-O2 section __TEXT,__text: 848 -> 768 (-80) section __TEXT,__unwind_info: 104 -> 96 (-8) symbol _tally_sum: 0x10000075c -> 0x100000740 ... recovered function starts: 6 -> 6 ``` The optimizer removed 80 bytes of code, so every function after `main` moved. The import list did not change. The diff of the unstripped and stripped builds lists eight removed exports: strip rewrote the exports trie of the executable down to `__mh_execute_header`. ```figure pj-binary-inspector-6 ``` In the lab, set the file size, the cell count, and a section range. The lab computes each cell range, the overlap, and the region the rule picks. ## Implement the contract `byte_map(...) -> list[dict]`: raise `ValueError` when `cells` is below 1. Use `min(cells, len(data))` cells, at least 1. Each item is `{"index", "offset", "length", "region", "entropy"}`. `build_report(...) -> dict` with exactly these top-level keys: | Key | Value | |---|---| | `schema` | `"binary-inspector/report/v1"` (`REPORT_SCHEMA`) | | `file` | `{"name", "size", "sha256"}` | | `header` | `parse_header` | | `sections`, `segments` | stage 2 | | `symbols` | stage 3 | | `imports`, `exports`, `relocations` | stage 4 | | `fixups` | the `fixups` list of `chained_fixups` | | `strings` | stage 5 with `min_string` | | `function_starts` | stage 5. When `truth` bytes are given, add `truth` (the `symbols` method of the truth file) and `scores` (one `score_starts` per method). | | `byte_map` | with `cells` | | `summary` | counts: `format`, `arch`, `kind`, `sections`, `segments`, `symbols`, `defined_functions`, `imports`, `exports`, `relocations`, `fixups`, `strings`, `recovered_starts`, `file_entropy` | The report must survive `json.dumps` with no custom encoder. The supplied JSON Schema file in the workspace documents the same shape for other tools. `validate_report(report) -> list[str]`: return `["report must be an object"]` for a non-dictionary. Otherwise check each key in `REPORT_FIELDS` with the messages `missing key ` and ` must be `, each list item in `ITEM_FIELDS` with `[] missing `, the three `file` fields, and `format`, `arch`, `kind` in `header`. `render_html(report) -> str`: start with ``. Include the summary and the byte map, with exactly one element with `class="cell"` per cell. Add one table each for sections, segments, function starts and scores, symbols, imports, exports, relocations, fixups, and strings. Escape every value with `html.escape`. Load no external script, style, or font. `diff_reports(old, new) -> dict`: raise `ValueError` when either report fails `validate_report`. Return: ```python {"schema": "binary-inspector/diff/v1", "old": {...}, "new": {...}, "identical": bool, "header_changes": {key: [old, new]}, "sections": {"added", "removed", "changed": [{"name", "old_size", "new_size", "delta", "old_entropy", "new_entropy"}]}, "symbols": {"added", "removed", "moved": [{"name", "old", "new"}]}, "imports": {"added", "removed"}, "exports": {"added", "removed"}, "strings": {"added", "removed"}, "function_starts": {"old", "new"}} ``` Name a Mach-O section `segment,section`. Sum the sizes of sections with the same name, because a COFF object has six sections called `.rdata`. Compare defined symbols only, without section and file symbols. `render_diff_text(diff) -> str`: first line `old -> new`, then `section NAME: OLD -> NEW (+/-DELTA)`, `symbol NAME: 0xOLD -> 0xNEW`, `+ kind name` and `- kind name` lines, and last `recovered function starts: OLD -> NEW`. ## Verify and inspect ```bash python3 scripts/project_test.py binary-inspector --all --path learning-artifacts/binary-inspector --strict cd learning-artifacts/binary-inspector python3 cli.py inspect fixtures/tally-arm64-O2.stripped --truth fixtures/tally-arm64-O2 --json report.json --html report.html python3 cli.py diff fixtures/tally-arm64-O0 fixtures/tally-arm64-O2 --json diff.json ``` The integration test runs your CLI on the held-out program and validates the JSON it writes. It also checks the exit code for a C source file. ## Investigate the failure boundary - Replace the string `unknown bucket` in a copy of the executable with `
